title: AI governance interview master

stops.title: How to use this doc
stops.contentMd:
## How to use this doc

The EY interview failed on recall, not knowledge: the material existed but could not be produced under pressure. So this doc is for drilling, not reading.

**Answer format for technical screens.** List first, then one line of example only if asked. When an interviewer says "just tell me", give names, not explanations.

**Drill protocol**

1. Read one layer. Close the doc. Say the answers out loud.
2. Type "drill me" in chat. Claude asks Layer 1 questions rapid-fire, times nothing but scores each answer: correct, partial, missed.
3. Missed items go back into the next drill until they are correct twice in a row.
4. After every real interview, add an entry to the Interview log and move any question you missed into Layer 1.

**Readiness bar before applying anywhere**

- [ ] Every Layer 1 answer given correctly, cold, in two consecutive drills
- [ ] Every CV claim in Layer 5 marked "keep" can be defended for 3 minutes
- [ ] CV fixes in Layer 5 applied
- [ ] 60-second intro delivered without notes
- [ ] One full mock interview (intro, Layer 1, one story, one scenario) passed
stops.artifactPrompt: Before reading any further stop, write out the 5-item readiness bar above as your own checklist, and date it. You'll come back and tick items off as you complete the rest of this module.

stops.title: Layer 1: 10-second answers
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 1: 10-second answers

These are the questions every AI governance screen opens with. Four of the five EY questions are here. Memorise the answer column almost word for word.

### Responsible AI

| # | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Principles of responsible AI? | Fairness and non-discrimination, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy and data governance, security and robustness, safety, human oversight, sustainability. |
| 2 | Where do those come from? | OECD AI Principles (5 values-based principles), the EU High-Level Expert Group's 7 requirements for Trustworthy AI, and NIST's 7 trustworthy characteristics. Most firms adapt one of these. |
| 3 | EU HLEG 7 requirements? | Human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental wellbeing; accountability. |
| 4 | Responsible AI in one line? | Designing, deploying and monitoring AI so it is fair, safe, transparent and accountable, with evidence to prove it. |

### EU AI Act

| # | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | EU AI Act in one line? | A risk-based EU law that classifies AI by the harm its use can cause: banned, high-risk, transparency-risk, or minimal. Obligations scale with the tier. |
| 6 | The tiers? | Prohibited (Art 5), high-risk (Art 6, Annex I and III), transparency obligations (Art 50), minimal risk. Plus a separate track for general-purpose AI models (Arts 51-56). |
| 7 | Name prohibited practices | Manipulative or subliminal techniques; exploiting vulnerabilities; social scoring; predictive policing on profiling alone; untargeted facial scraping; emotion recognition at work or school; biometric categorisation by sensitive traits; real-time remote biometric ID in public for police (narrow exceptions). From Dec 2026: AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM. |
| 8 | What makes a system high-risk? | Route 1: safety component of a product under EU product law (Annex I). Route 2: use in an Annex III area: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services incl. credit scoring and life/health insurance, law enforcement, migration, justice and democracy. |
| 9 | Provider vs deployer? | Provider builds or puts it on the market under its name and carries most duties (Arts 9-17). Deployer uses it professionally: follow instructions, human oversight, monitoring, logs, and an FRIA for credit and insurance (Arts 26-27). |
| 10 | Key dates? | In force Aug 2024. Bans and AI literacy Feb 2025. GPAI Aug 2025. Transparency Aug 2026. Annex III high-risk Dec 2027 and Annex I Aug 2028 (delayed by the 2026 Digital Omnibus). |
| 11 | Fines? | Up to 35m euro or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices; 15m or 3% for most other breaches; 7.5m or 1% for misleading information. |
| 12 | Does it apply to a UK bank? | Only where the system is placed on the EU market or its output is used in the EU. Many UK firms still use it as the benchmark. |

### Frameworks and standards

| # | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13 | NIST AI RMF in one line? | A voluntary US framework (Jan 2023) for managing AI risk through four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. |
| 14 | What does each function do? | Govern: culture, policy, accountability (cross-cutting). Map: context and risk identification. Measure: test, evaluate, monitor. Manage: prioritise, treat, respond. |
| 15 | NIST trustworthy characteristics? | Valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed. |
| 16 | NIST GenAI profile? | NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024). 12 GenAI risks, e.g. confabulation, information integrity, data privacy, information security, IP, harmful bias. |
| 17 | ISO 42001 in one line? | The certifiable international standard for an AI Management System: how an organisation governs AI and proves it to an auditor. |
| 18 | ISO 42001 structure? | Clauses 4-10 (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement). Annex A: 38 controls across 9 objectives. Statement of Applicability. |
| 19 | Risk vs impact assessment in 42001? | Risk assessment (6.1.2): risk to the organisation. Impact assessment (6.1.4): consequences for individuals and society. |
| 20 | How do the three fit together? | ISO 42001 is the management system, NIST is the risk method inside it, the EU AI Act is the legal floor. |
| 21 | OWASP LLM Top 10, first five? | Prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling. (Then excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation, unbounded consumption.) |
| 22 | MITRE ATLAS? | A knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on MITRE ATT&CK. Used for threat modelling and red-team scope. |

### Risks and controls

| # | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 23 | Monitoring or observability controls for an AI system? | Performance against baseline with thresholds; data and concept drift; hallucination or groundedness rate; fairness metrics over time; human override rate; guardrail and PII-leak triggers; latency, errors and cost; complaints and incidents. Each with a threshold, an alert and an owner. |
| 24 | What is RAG and its main risks? | Retrieval-augmented generation: the model answers from retrieved documents. Risks: hallucination beyond the source, stale or unapproved content, access leakage across permissions, prompt injection via documents. |
| 25 | Data drift vs concept drift? | Data drift: input distribution changes. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes. |
| 26 | Fairness metrics? | Demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalised odds. They can conflict, so choosing one is a documented business decision. |
| 27 | Explainability types? | Global (how the model works overall) vs local (why this decision). Tools: SHAP, LIME; citations for RAG. |
| 28 | Human oversight models? | Human-in-the-loop (approves each output), human-on-the-loop (monitors, can intervene), human-in-command (decides whether to use it at all). |
| 29 | What goes in an AI inventory? | Owner, purpose, model type, vendor, data used, risk tier, deployment status, last review date. |
| 30 | Three lines of defence for AI? | 1LOD business owns the risk and runs controls; 2LOD risk and compliance set the framework and challenge; 3LOD internal audit gives independent assurance. |
| 31 | Agentic AI: what changes? | Risk moves from outputs to actions. Controls: agent identity with least privilege, human approval for high-impact actions, tool-call logging, staged autonomy, kill switch. |

### Privacy and India

| # | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32 | GDPR and AI? | Lawful basis, data minimisation, DPIA (Art 35) for high-risk processing, and Art 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. |
| 33 | DPDP status? | DPDP Act passed 2023. Rules notified Nov 2025, phased in, most obligations about 18 months later. |
| 34 | RBI FREE-AI? | RBI's Aug 2025 framework for responsible AI in finance: 7 sutras, 6 pillars, 26 recommendations, including a board-approved AI policy, AI in audit scope, and AI incident reporting. |
| 35 | MeitY AI Governance Guidelines? | Nov 2025. No umbrella AI law; 7 sutras; sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI) set sector rules; proposes an AI Governance Group and AI Safety Institute. |

quiz.question: Principles of responsible AI?
quiz.answer: Fairness and non-discrimination, transparency, explainability, accountability, privacy and data governance, security and robustness, safety, human oversight, sustainability.
quiz.explanation: The master list every screen opens with — must be cold, no hesitation.

quiz.question: Where do those come from?
quiz.answer: OECD AI Principles (5 values-based principles), the EU High-Level Expert Group's 7 requirements for Trustworthy AI, and NIST's 7 trustworthy characteristics. Most firms adapt one of these.
quiz.explanation: Naming sources, not just the list, signals depth.

quiz.question: EU HLEG 7 requirements?
quiz.answer: Human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental wellbeing; accountability.
quiz.explanation: The value base the EU AI Act was built on.

quiz.question: Responsible AI in one line?
quiz.answer: Designing, deploying and monitoring AI so it is fair, safe, transparent and accountable, with evidence to prove it.
quiz.explanation: The crispest possible answer to an open-ended opener.

quiz.question: EU AI Act in one line?
quiz.answer: A risk-based EU law that classifies AI by the harm its use can cause: banned, high-risk, transparency-risk, or minimal. Obligations scale with the tier.
quiz.explanation: Lead with this before any article numbers.

quiz.question: The EU AI Act tiers?
quiz.answer: Prohibited (Art 5), high-risk (Art 6, Annex I and III), transparency obligations (Art 50), minimal risk. Plus a separate track for general-purpose AI models (Arts 51-56).
quiz.explanation: GPAI is a separate track, not a fifth tier — a common trap.

quiz.question: Name the EU AI Act's prohibited practices.
quiz.answer: Manipulative or subliminal techniques; exploiting vulnerabilities; social scoring; predictive policing on profiling alone; untargeted facial scraping; emotion recognition at work or school; biometric categorisation by sensitive traits; real-time remote biometric ID in public for police (narrow exceptions). From Dec 2026: AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery or CSAM.
quiz.explanation: A ban cannot be mitigated — this list is worth knowing precisely.

quiz.question: What makes an EU AI Act system high-risk?
quiz.answer: Route 1: safety component of a product under EU product law (Annex I). Route 2: use in an Annex III area: biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services incl. credit scoring and life/health insurance, law enforcement, migration, justice and democracy.
quiz.explanation: Two independent routes into high-risk — know both.

quiz.question: Provider vs deployer under the EU AI Act?
quiz.answer: Provider builds or puts it on the market under its name and carries most duties (Arts 9-17). Deployer uses it professionally: follow instructions, human oversight, monitoring, logs, and an FRIA for credit and insurance (Arts 26-27).
quiz.explanation: A deployer that substantially modifies a system becomes the provider.

quiz.question: EU AI Act key dates?
quiz.answer: In force Aug 2024. Bans and AI literacy Feb 2025. GPAI Aug 2025. Transparency Aug 2026. Annex III high-risk Dec 2027 and Annex I Aug 2028 (delayed by the 2026 Digital Omnibus).
quiz.explanation: Re-check these before quoting them — the Digital Omnibus already moved one date.

quiz.question: EU AI Act fines?
quiz.answer: Up to 35m euro or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices; 15m or 3% for most other breaches; 7.5m or 1% for misleading information.
quiz.explanation: Three tiers of fines matching the severity of the breach.

quiz.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to a UK bank?
quiz.answer: Only where the system is placed on the EU market or its output is used in the EU. Many UK firms still use it as the benchmark.
quiz.explanation: Extraterritorial scope is narrower than people assume — a frequent trap question.

quiz.question: NIST AI RMF in one line?
quiz.answer: A voluntary US framework (Jan 2023) for managing AI risk through four functions: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.
quiz.explanation: Say these four words cold, every time.

quiz.question: What does each NIST function do?
quiz.answer: Govern: culture, policy, accountability (cross-cutting). Map: context and risk identification. Measure: test, evaluate, monitor. Manage: prioritise, treat, respond.
quiz.explanation: Govern sits above the other three, which loop per system.

quiz.question: NIST's trustworthy characteristics?
quiz.answer: Valid and reliable; safe; secure and resilient; accountable and transparent; explainable and interpretable; privacy-enhanced; fair with harmful bias managed.
quiz.explanation: Valid and reliable is the foundation — nothing else matters if the system doesn't work.

quiz.question: NIST's GenAI profile?
quiz.answer: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024). 12 GenAI risks, e.g. confabulation, information integrity, data privacy, information security, IP, harmful bias.
quiz.explanation: The go-to reference for any GenAI-specific assessment.

quiz.question: ISO 42001 in one line?
quiz.answer: The certifiable international standard for an AI Management System: how an organisation governs AI and proves it to an auditor.
quiz.explanation: Certifiable is the key word — it's what makes 42001 different from NIST.

quiz.question: ISO 42001 structure?
quiz.answer: Clauses 4-10 (context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement). Annex A: 38 controls across 9 objectives. Statement of Applicability.
quiz.explanation: Clauses are mandatory; only Annex A controls can be excluded.

quiz.question: Risk vs impact assessment in ISO 42001?
quiz.answer: Risk assessment (6.1.2): risk to the organisation. Impact assessment (6.1.4): consequences for individuals and society.
quiz.explanation: The impact assessment result feeds the risk assessment, not the reverse.

quiz.question: How do ISO 42001, NIST and the EU AI Act fit together?
quiz.answer: ISO 42001 is the management system, NIST is the risk method inside it, the EU AI Act is the legal floor.
quiz.explanation: The single most useful one-liner for tying the three frameworks together in an answer.

quiz.question: OWASP LLM Top 10, first five?
quiz.answer: Prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling. (Then excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation, unbounded consumption.)
quiz.explanation: Know the first five cold; the rest can be named as 'then...' if pushed.

quiz.question: What is MITRE ATLAS?
quiz.answer: A knowledge base of real attacker tactics and techniques against AI systems, modelled on MITRE ATT&CK. Used for threat modelling and red-team scope.
quiz.explanation: Pairs with OWASP for a complete security-testing answer.

quiz.question: Monitoring or observability controls for an AI system?
quiz.answer: Performance against baseline with thresholds; data and concept drift; hallucination or groundedness rate; fairness metrics over time; human override rate; guardrail and PII-leak triggers; latency, errors and cost; complaints and incidents. Each with a threshold, an alert and an owner.
quiz.explanation: This exact question is the one the EY interview was lost on — know it cold.

quiz.question: What is RAG and its main risks?
quiz.answer: Retrieval-augmented generation: the model answers from retrieved documents. Risks: hallucination beyond the source, stale or unapproved content, access leakage across permissions, prompt injection via documents.
quiz.explanation: Spell out the full term once, then use 'RAG' freely.

quiz.question: Data drift vs concept drift?
quiz.answer: Data drift: input distribution changes. Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes.
quiz.explanation: A classic pair that's easy to blur under pressure.

quiz.question: Fairness metrics?
quiz.answer: Demographic parity, equal opportunity, equalised odds. They can conflict, so choosing one is a documented business decision.
quiz.explanation: Naming the conflict unprompted shows practitioner-level understanding.

quiz.question: Explainability types?
quiz.answer: Global (how the model works overall) vs local (why this decision). Tools: SHAP, LIME; citations for RAG.
quiz.explanation: Global vs local is the key distinction interviewers probe.

quiz.question: Human oversight models?
quiz.answer: Human-in-the-loop (approves each output), human-on-the-loop (monitors, can intervene), human-in-command (decides whether to use it at all).
quiz.explanation: Three distinct levels of human involvement, each suited to a different risk tier.

quiz.question: What goes in an AI inventory?
quiz.answer: Owner, purpose, model type, vendor, data used, risk tier, deployment status, last review date.
quiz.explanation: The foundation every other governance activity depends on.

quiz.question: Three lines of defence for AI?
quiz.answer: 1LOD business owns the risk and runs controls; 2LOD risk and compliance set the framework and challenge; 3LOD internal audit gives independent assurance.
quiz.explanation: Know which line you personally sat in — it's almost always asked as a follow-up.

quiz.question: Agentic AI: what changes?
quiz.answer: Risk moves from outputs to actions. Controls: agent identity with least privilege, human approval for high-impact actions, tool-call logging, staged autonomy, kill switch.
quiz.explanation: The shift from 'wrong words' to 'wrong actions' is the core idea to lead with.

quiz.question: GDPR and AI?
quiz.answer: Lawful basis, data minimisation, DPIA (Art 35) for high-risk processing, and Art 22: right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects.
quiz.explanation: Article 22 is the one most often forgotten under pressure.

quiz.question: DPDP status?
quiz.answer: DPDP Act passed 2023. Rules notified Nov 2025, phased in, most obligations about 18 months later.
quiz.explanation: India's privacy law timeline — re-check before quoting, as with all dates.

quiz.question: RBI FREE-AI?
quiz.answer: RBI's Aug 2025 framework for responsible AI in finance: 7 sutras, 6 pillars, 26 recommendations, including a board-approved AI policy, AI in audit scope, and AI incident reporting.
quiz.explanation: The anchor framework for any Indian bank conversation.

quiz.question: MeitY AI Governance Guidelines?
quiz.answer: Nov 2025. No umbrella AI law; 7 sutras; sector regulators (RBI, SEBI, IRDAI) set sector rules; proposes an AI Governance Group and AI Safety Institute.
quiz.explanation: India's approach is deliberately sector-led rather than one umbrella law, unlike the EU.

stops.artifactPrompt: Close this stop. Say all 35 answers out loud from memory, in order, timing yourself only to notice where you hesitate. Write down every number you missed or fumbled, then re-drill just those until each is correct twice in a row, per the drill protocol.

stops.title: Layer 2: Core frameworks
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 2: Core frameworks

Depth for the follow-up questions. Know the why behind each: it lets you rebuild the detail under pressure.

### EU AI Act: Article map

Why it exists: the EU regulates AI like a product (prove it is safe before it reaches the market), and scales the burden to the risk the use creates for people.

| Article | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | Definitions, incl. AI system, provider, deployer |
| 4 | AI literacy for staff of providers and deployers (from Feb 2025) |
| 5 | Prohibited practices |
| 6 + Annex I, III | High-risk classification. 6(3): an Annex III system is not high-risk if it only does a narrow procedural, improving, pattern-detecting or preparatory task, unless it profiles people |
| 9 | Risk management system across the lifecycle |
| 10 | Data and data governance, incl. bias examination |
| 11 + Annex IV | Technical documentation |
| 12 | Record-keeping (logs) |
| 13 | Transparency and instructions for use, from provider to deployer |
| 14 | Human oversight |
| 15 | Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity |
| 17 | Quality management system (where ISO 42001 helps most) |
| 25 | A deployer that substantially modifies a system or rebrands it becomes the provider |
| 26 | Deployer obligations |
| 27 | Fundamental rights impact assessment (public bodies, public services, credit scoring, life and health insurance) |
| 43, 47, 48, 49 | Conformity assessment, declaration of conformity, CE marking, EU database registration |
| 50 | Transparency: disclose chatbots, mark synthetic content, inform people exposed to emotion recognition, label deepfakes |
| 51-56 | General-purpose AI models; systemic risk presumed above 10^25 FLOPs of training compute |
| 72, 73 | Post-market monitoring; serious incident reporting (15 days, 10 for a death, 2 for widespread or critical infrastructure) |
| 86 | Right to an explanation of high-risk AI decisions |
| 99, 101 | Penalties; GPAI fines |

One trap worth knowing: emotion recognition means inference from biometric data such as voice or face. Sentiment analysis of typed text is not covered. Detecting customer frustration from voice is high-risk (Annex III 1(c)), not banned; doing it to employees is banned.

### NIST AI RMF

Why it exists: a voluntary, outcome-based way to think about AI risk. It is strong on method and weak on audit evidence, so pair it with ISO 42001.

| Function | Categories | Key content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Govern | 6 | Policies, accountability, workforce diversity, risk culture, stakeholder engagement, third-party risk |
| Map | 5 | Context and purpose, categorisation, benefits and costs, third-party components, impacts on people |
| Measure | 4 | Methods and metrics, evaluation against trustworthy characteristics, tracking risk over time, feedback on measurement |
| Manage | 4 | Prioritise and respond, maximise benefit and minimise harm, third-party risk, treatment and communication |

19 categories, 72 subcategories. The trustworthy characteristics trade off: more explainability can cost accuracy, privacy techniques can limit fairness testing. Governance records(who made the trade-off).

### ISO/IEC 42001:2023

Why it exists: the first certifiable AI management system standard. It does for AI what ISO 27001 did for security: makes "we govern AI responsibly" auditable.

| Annex A | Control objective |
| --- | --- |
| A.2 | Policies related to AI |
| A.3 | Internal organisation (roles, reporting concerns) |
| A.4 | Resources for AI systems (data, tooling, compute, people) |
| A.5 | Assessing impacts of AI systems |
| A.6 | AI system life cycle (requirements to monitoring, documentation, event logs) |
| A.7 | Data for AI systems ((quality, provenance, preparation) |
| A.8 | Information for interested parties (user docs, incident communication) |
| A.9 | Use of AI systems (responsible use, intended use) |
| A.10 | Third-party and customer relationships |

Annex B gives implementation guidance; Annex C lists AI objectives and risk sources; Annex D covers sectors. Related standards: 22989 (terms), 23894 (AI risk guidance), 42005 (impact assessment), 42006 (certification bodies). Certification: Stage 1 audit (documents), Stage 2 (operating evidence), 3-year certificate with annual surveillance.

### Security: OWASP and MITRE ATLAS

Governance owns the oversight, security owns the testing. Require ATLAS-based threat modelling at design, OWASP test coverage evidence before go-live, findings tracked to closure.

**OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications (Dec 2025):** agent goal hijack, tool misuse, identity and privilege abuse, agentic supply chain, unexpected code execution, memory and context poisoning, insecure inter-agent communication, cascading failures, human-agent trust exploitation, rogue agents.

### India

| Instrument | Status | Use in an answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MeitY AI Governance Guidelines | Nov 2025, voluntary | No umbrella AI law; sector regulators lead |
| RBI FREE-AI | Aug 2025 | Anchor for any Indian bank: board-approved AI policy, AI in audit scope, incident reporting |
| DPDP Act and Rules | Act 2023, Rules Nov 2025, phased | Consent, purpose limitation, rights, breach notification for AI using personal data |
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick 3 EU AI Act article numbers from the map above and, without looking, write one sentence each on what they cover. Then check yourself against the table. Repeat for the ISO 42001 Annex A objectives you're least confident on.

stops.title: Layer 3: Controls library
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 3: Controls library

At EY you answered a monitoring question with a design control. Know the difference: a **design control** shapes the system before it runs (preventive). A **monitoring control** tells you it is misbehaving once it runs (detective). Monitoring sits in NIST Measure and Manage.

### Monitoring and observability controls

| Control | What it watches | Example threshold and action | NIST |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Performance monitoring | Accuracy, precision, recall against the validated baseline | Drop of more than 5 points vs baseline: alert model owner, review within 5 days | Measure 4, Manage 4 |
| Data drift | Shift in input distribution (e.g. PSI) | PSI above 0.25: alert, retraining review | Measure 2 |
| Concept drift | Outcome relationship changes (rising errors on labelled samples) | Error trend breach on monthly sample: review | Measure 2 |
| Hallucination / groundedness | Claims in the answer not supported by retrieved sources | Groundedness below agreed rate on weekly sample: alert, restrict topic | Measure 2 |
| Retrieval quality (RAG) | Queries with no relevant document found | Failure rate above 5% on regulated topics: knowledge base gap review | Measure 2 |
| Fairness over time | Outcome disparity across groups | Disparity beyond agreed limit: escalate to model risk | Measure 2.11 |
| Human oversight effectiveness | Override rate, source-verification rate | 0% overrides or verification below 80%: oversight review, retraining of staff | Manage 2 |
| Guardrail triggers | Blocked prompts, jailbreak attemps, toxic output | Spike vs baseline: security review | Measure 2.7 |
| PII leakage | Personal data in outputs or logs | Any confirmed case: incident, 24h containment | Manage 4 |
| Operational health | Latency, error rate, availability, token cost | SLA breach or cost spike: ops alert, fallback proces | Manage 2 |
| Outcome signals | Complaints, escalations, ticket volumes linked to AI answers | 20% month-on-month rise: governance review | Manage 4 |
| Logging and traceability | Every input, retrieved source, output and model version stored | Log gaps: control failure | Measure, Govern |

Every monitoring control needs four things: a metric, a threshold, an alert route, and a named owner with a response deadline. Without the last two it is a dashboard, not a control.

### Model answer to the EY question

"I'd set monitoring at three levels. Model: performance against baseline, drift, and for GenAI a groundedness rate on sampled answers. Human: override and verification rates, to prove oversight actually happens. Outcome: complaints and escalations linked to AI answers. Each has a threshold, an automated alert and an owner who must respond within a set time. Breaches feed the incident process and trigger re-assessment."

### Design controls (preventive)

| Control | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Intake and risk tiering before build | Nothing reaches production unassessed |
| Impact assessment / DPIA | Harm to people identified before launch |
| Data quality and provenance check | Bias and error caught at source |
| Pre-deployment validation and red-team evidence | Performance and security proven before go-live |
| Grounding with source citations | Answers traceable to approved content |
| Knowledge base approval workflow, owners, 48-hour update SLA | Only current, approved content is retrievable |
| Human approval for high-impact outputs or agent actions | Oversight by design |
| Release gate requiring 2LOD sign-off for high tier | Decision rights enforced |
| Vendor contract clauses: no training on client data, change notice, audit rights | Third-party risk controlled |

### Writing a good control

Owner, activity, frequency, method, evidence, preventive or detective, manual or automated, risk mitigated. Test design effectiveness (would it work as written?) separately from operating effectiveness (did it run, every time?).
stops.artifactPrompt: Memorise the model answer to the EY question word for word, then deliver it out loud from memory, unscripted, in under 45 seconds. Record yourself if you can, and check you named all three levels (model, human, outcome) and both missing pieces (alert, owner with deadline).

stops.title: Layer 4: Project stories
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 4: Project stories

Four Barclays projects, all in the 1LOD Chief Controls Office. You assessed governance during pilots; you did not build any system. Say "RAG assistant" clearly, and spell out "retrieval-augmented generation" once.

| Question type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Assess a GenAI or RAG system | Help Hub |
| Design KRIs or monitoring | Help Hub, then Mortgage selector |
| Impact you had, a gap you found and fixed | Mortgage selector |
| Bias, NLP, thresholds, feedback loops | Call summarisation |
| Controls testing rigour, zero-tolerance outputs | COI automation |

### 1. Help Hub RAG assistant (lead story)

**S.** Agents searched Help Hub pages and 100-page policy PDFs during live calls, or raised tickets to experts while customers waited. A RAG assistant was piloted: question in, answer from Help Hub and lending and regulatory policy, with a source link.

**T.** Assess governance in the pilot. A wrong lending rule relayed to a customer is the bank's misleading communication, whoever generated it.

**A.** NIST AI RMF, three risks: hallucination on regulated content when no document matches; knowledge base governance (anyone could upload, no approval, drafts and old versions retrievable, no update SLA); optional source verification on live calls.

**R.** Three findings mapped to FCA Consumer Duty and DISP: hallucination testing on regulated queries before go-live and after major updates; named document owners, compliance approval, 48-hour update SLA, retire old versions; mandatory logged verification with a verification-rate KRI (below 80% triggers retraining).

**Monitoring follow-up (the EY miss):** knowledge base currency lag vs 48-hour SLA; verification rate; expert ticket escalation rate (20% month-on-month rise triggers review); query failure rate (above 5% on regulated topics); complaints citing wrong agent information.

**Lesson.** An optional check isn't a control. Look at whether oversight happens, not whether it exists.

Open question: were the findings adopted? If unknown, say "I escalated them; adoption sat with the business."

### 2. Mortgage rate selector (best result story)

**S.** Digital pilot: a 90-day rule found customers near fixed-rate expiry; an Automated Valuation Model (AVM, an ML model) plus outstanding balance gave the LTV; LTV mapped to four brackets; the app showed eligible deals.

**T.** Assess controls at each pipeline stage.

**A.** Mapped the pipeline and named the AVM as the highest-risk component. Reconciled a risk-based sample of system LTVs against core banking data. Checked every eligible deal was returned. Contact-centre calls from this segment were higher than expected; root cause: customers never saw the AVM valuation or balance that decided their deals, so they couldn't check or challenge it.

**R.** The team added an LTV breakdown (valuation, balance, ratio) and a query route for disputed valuations, and logged which AVM output was used. Calls from the segment fell. KRIs set for LTV accuracy, deal completeness, query rate, call rate and bracket misclassification.

**Say this, not that.** Basis: FCA Consumer Duty, consumer understanding outcome. Use the EU AI Act only as a benchmark (UK bank, UK customers; Article 13 is provider-to-deployer, customer explanation is Article 86). An AVM is not formally creditworthiness evaluation under Annex III 5(b).

### 3. Call summarisation and NLP detection

**S.** Three components on call audio: speech-to-text plus summarisation; real-time complaint and dissatisfaction alerts; real-time vulnerability alerts. Before, agents took manual notes and disclosures were missed.

**T.** Assess governance of each component against DISP, Consumer Vulnerability Guidance and Consumer Duty.

**A and R.** Four findings:

- Speech-to-text accuracy had to be tested across accents and non-native speakers before rollout, because errors flow into complaint and vulnerability detection.
- Agent ratings fed retraining with no review: if agents rate disclosure-heavy summaries lower, the model learns to under-report. Recommended a governance gate before feedback enters retraining.
- Complaint and vulnerability thresholds were set by engineering on aggregate accuracy. Under DISP a missed complaint is a breach, so recall matters more than precision; the threshold must be a documented risk-appetite decision owned by compliance.
- The vulnerability trigger set was defined by the tech team without safeguarding input. Recommended compliance ownership and annual review against the FCA's four drivers: health, life events, resilience, capability.

**Depth point.** Under the EU AI Act, detecting dissatisfaction from voice tone would be emotion recognition (high-risk); from transcript text it would not.

### 4. COI automation (controls rigour)

**S.** Automated year-end Certificates of Interest that customers use for tax filing. Acceptable error: zero.

**A.** Tested each of three stages independently: extraction (only interest transaction codes, sample across five account types), calculation (test cases per scenario), PDF generation ((printed figure matches calculated figure).

**R.** Found a boundary-date edge case that would have understated interest for accounts with last-day-of-tax-year entries. Fixed before production.

**Say this, not that.** It is deterministic automation, not AI. "The control discipline is identical: test each stage, reconcile, keep the audit trail."
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick one of your own past projects, however small, and write it up in the exact S/T/A/R format used here (Situation, Task, Action, Result), aiming for the same density of specific detail (names, numbers, named controls) as the Help Hub story.

stops.title: Layer 5: CV defence
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 5: CV defence

Ketan read your CV line by line and probed each claim. Every line must survive three follow-ups. Rule: if you can't defend it for 3 minutes, reword it or cut it.

**Fix first (typos):** "sAJAY" at the top, "PROFESSIONAL EXPERIE" header cut off, "Pursing" in the profile.

| Claim on CV | Likely follow-up | Your answer or the fix | Action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Profile: "ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management Systems and Pursing IAPP AIGP" | "Are you certified? Name the clauses." | Reads as if you hold 42001. Change to "Studying ISO/IEC 42001 (AIQI Consortium) and pursuing IAPP AIGP". | Reword |
| Profile and Key Knowledge Areas: EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, GDPR | The four EY questions | Layer 1 answers 5-20 and 32. Keep only once you pass them cold. | Verify |
| Help Hub: model temperature set for variety, recommended near zero | "What value was it? How did you see the config? Why does temperature matter?" | Not in your Q&A doc. Keep only if you saw the setting. Answer: temperature controls randomness in word selection; near zero gives consistent answers to the same question, which regulated guidance needs. | Verify |
| Help Hub: optional source link "does not satisfy human oversight under EU AI Act Article 14 for High-Risk AI in financial services" | "Is Help Hub high-risk? Does the Act apply to Barclays UK?" | Wrong on both. Reword: "...did not provide effective human oversight ((benchmarked against EU AI Act Article 14). | Reword |
| Call AI: "identifying that ASR transcription accuracy degraded across customer demographics" | "By how much? How was it measured?" | Your Q&A doc says you assessed whether it had been tested. Reword: "identified that ASR accuracy had not been benchmarked across demographics". | Reword |
| Call AI: "agent rating data trended lower for summaries containing complaint and vulnerability content" | "What data showed that?" | Your Q&A doc says nobody was monitoring it. Reword to "identified the risk that..." unless you saw the data. | Reword |
| Call AI: thresholds set by engineering, compliance ownership required | "Precision vs recall: which matters and why?" | Consistent with your Q&A doc. Recall, because a missed complaint is a DISP breach. | Keep |
| Controls testing: "sustaining 85-90% accuracy across regulatory checks" | "Accuracy of what? So 10-15% were wrong?" | Ambiguous and reads as your error rate. State what it measured, or cut the number. | Reword |
| "Built KRI-driven MI ... single source of truth for controls governance" | "So you built the AI monitoring dashboard?" | EY probed this and you said "not fully". It was controls-testing MI, not AI monitoring. Prepare 3 examples (e.g. exception rate by type, late or unreported items, remediation ageing). Reword to "controls testing MI". | Reword |
| "Designed leading indicators and lag KPIs ... PDCA" | "Give me one leading and one lagging indicator." | Prepare two real examples, or cut. | Verify |
| Competency: AI Audit and Independent Model Review Planning | "Which audit did you plan?" | No evidence in your experience. | Cut |
| Competency: Model Risk: Bias, Drift, Explainability and Fairness Evaluation | "How do you measure drift? Which fairness metric?" | Partial evidence (ASR bias). Keep only after Layer 1 answers 25-27. | Verify |
| Competency: GenAI, Agentic AI and MCP architectures | "What is MCP and its risks?" | Model Context Protocol: an open standard connecting AI agents to tools and data. Risks: over-permissioned servers, malicious tools, prompt injection through tool outputs. | Verify |
| Competency: Cloud governance and SOC audit familiarity | "SOC 1 vs SOC 2? Type 1 vs Type 2?" | SOC 1: controls over financial reporting. SOC 2: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy. Type 1: design at a point in time; Type 2: operation over a period. Keep only if you can say this. | Verify |
| Competency: GDPR, FCA, AML/KYC | "What AML/KYC work did you do?" | No AML/KYC evidence in your roles. | Reword |
| Tools: SQL, Tableau, ServiceNow, ALM/ADO/Jira "conceptual" | "What did you build in SQL or Tableau?" | "Conceptual" invites the question. List only tools you used. | Reword |
| TJX: fraud reports down 12%, shrinkage down 8% | "How did you measure it, and what was your part?" | Keep if you can explain the baseline and your role. | Keep |
| Missing: current role at Cursory (AI governance platform) and independent consulting | "What have you done since April 2026?" | Your CV ends in Apr 2026. Add the current role. | Add |
| Missing: Mortgage rate selector | "Tell me about an impact you had." | Your strongest result: explainability gap found, fix shipped, calls fell. Add one bullet. | Add |
stops.artifactPrompt: Go line by line through your own current CV the way Ketan did here. For each claim, write the likely follow-up question and whether you'd keep, reword, cut, or add. Do this before any real interview, not during one.

stops.title: Layer 6: Consulting scenarios
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 6: Consulting scenarios

Big 4 interviews test whether you can advise a client, not recite law. Structure every answer: classify, check the obligations, give options, name who decides.

### 1. "Our use case is prohibited, but we want to keep it and stay compliant" (Ketan's example)

1. Confirm it really is prohibited. Each Article 5 ban has precise conditions: 5(1)(a) needs material distortion of behaviour and significant harm; 5(1)(f) covers only workplaces and education, with a medical or safety exception; 5(1)(h) covers only real-time police use in public. Use the Commission's Article 5 guidelines (Feb 2025).
2. If it is in scope, there is no compliance route. A ban cannot be mitigated.
3. Redesign so it falls outside the ban: change the purpose, the population or the data. Example: emotion recognition on call-centre staff (banned) becomes call-quality analytics on transcript text (not biometric, so not emotion recognition).
4. Or limit it geographically: no EU market and no output used in the EU.
5. Document the legal analysis, get legal sign-off, and monitor for scope creep. Renaming the feature is not redesign.

### 2. "Assess us against the EU AI Act"

1. Build or validate the AI inventory.
2. For each system: role (provider or deployer) and tier.
3. Map the obligations per tier and role.
4. Review evidence against each obligation; rate the gaps.
5. Roadmap to the dates: bans already apply, transparency Aug 2026, Annex III Dec 2027, Annex I Aug 2028.

### 3. "Our credit scoring model: what do we need?"

Annex III 5(b), high-risk; fraud detection is excluded. If built in-house you are the provider: Articles 9-15, QMS, conformity assessment, CE marking, registration. If bought in you are a deployer: Article 26 duties and an Article 27 FRIA. Applies from 2 Dec 2027.

### 4. "We want a customer GenAI chatbot live in 4 weeks"

Don't block it. Tier it high (customer-facing, scale). Fast-track: scope limits, DPIA, groundedness testing, OWASP coverage evidence, Article 50 AI disclosure, human escalation, kill switch, monitoring from day one. Offer a reduced-scope launch (FAQs, no account advice) or a limited pilot. Residual risk accepted by the right approver.

### 5. "We have no AI governance. Where do we start?" (90 days)

- Days 1-30: inventory sprint, stakeholder interviews, maturity baseline, GenAI acceptable-use policy, interim approval route.
- Days 31-60: policy, risk tiering, taxonomy mapped into enterprise risk, RACI and decision rights, steering committee charter.
- Days 61-90: pilot assessments on 2-3 live use cases, control library, training plan, roadmap (and ISO 42001 path if wanted).

### 6. "We're rolling out a vendor AI tool to all staff"

Due diligence (training data, testing, security, data use, certifications), contract clauses ( no training on our data, change notice, audit rights, incident notice, data residency), inventory entry, acceptable-use training, usage monitoring. Accountability stays with the client.

### 7. "We're piloting an agent that can make payments"

Agent identity with least privilege, payment limits, human approval above a threshold, every tool call logged, staged autonomy, kill switch, test scope from the OWASP Agentic Top 10. The business owner is accountable for the agent's actions.

### 8. "We found 40 unapproved AI tools in use"

Amnesty to register them, risk-tier each, block the high-risk ones, provide approved alternatives, acceptable-use policy, network or CASB monitoring for new ones. Shadow AI usually means the approved route is too slow.
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick 2 of these 8 scenarios. Before reading the model answer again, write your own answer from scratch using the structure (classify, check obligations, give options, name who decides). Then compare against the model answer and note what you missed.

stops.title: Layer 7: Conduct
stops.contentMd:
## Layer 7: Conduct

At EY, conduct cost as much as knowledge: the interviewer suspected reading, heard "to be honest" repeatedly, and was told you weren't ready.

### 60-second intro ( say it, don't read it)

"I'm Ajay. I work where risk controls meet AI. At Barclays UK I was in the first-line Chief Controls Office, assessing governance on three AI pilots: a RAG policy assistant for lending agents, call summarisation with complaint and vulnerability detection, and a mortgage rate selector driven by a valuation model, where I found an explainability gap that was fixed and reduced call volumes. Before that I worked in fraud risk at TJX Europe. Since moving back to India I've worked with an AI governance platform, meeting CROs and CISOs at BFSI firms, so I see how far AI adoption is running ahead of governance. I want to move into advisory: designing and assessing those frameworks for clients."

### Rules

- No "to be honest" or "to be frank". It implies the rest wasn't.
- Speak slower than feels natural. Pause before answering.
- One-line question, one-line answer. List questions get lists.
- Don't know it? "I don't know that precisely. What I do know is..." Never "I'm not ready."
- Never reject yourself. At "any questions?", always ask one.
- Screen hygiene before the call: one screen, extensions and notes closed, camera on. If asked to share, do it calmly, as you did.

### Tricky questions

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| "Have you worked on the EU AI Act?" | "Not as a legal obligation: Barclays UK wasn't in scope. I used it as the benchmark in assessments, for example human oversight on the RAG pilot. In short, it's a risk-based law with four tiers..." |
| "Did you build the governance dashboard?" | "I built the controls-testing MI in Excel. On the AI pilots I defined the KRIs and thresholds; engineering implemented the monitoring." |
| "What have you done since April?" | "Enterprise work with an AI governance platform for BFSI clients, plus independent AI governance consulting." |
| "Do you have other offers? Are you offer shopping?" | "I'm in a few conversations. This role is my priority because it's pure AI governance advisory." No details, no stories. |
| "Why AIGP before mastering the basics?" | Avoid by passing Layer 1. If asked: "AIGP is how I'm structuring the fundamentals," then prove it with a crisp answer. |
| "Why consulting rather than in-house?" | "I've seen the in-house first-line view at Barclays and the vendor view selling a platform. Advisory is where both meet, and breadth across clients builds expertise faster." |
| "Your AI governance experience is under 4 years" | "AI governance is risk and controls discipline applied to a new technology. I have that discipline from a G-SIB, plus live AI pilot assessments." |

### Questions to ask

- What does a typical engagement look like: framework design, assessments, or certification readiness?
- Which sectors make up most of the AI governance client base?
- How does the practice split work between governance and technical AI assurance?
- What would success look like in the first six months?

quiz.question: "Have you worked on the EU AI Act?"
quiz.answer: "Not as a legal obligation: Barclays UK wasn't in scope. I used it as the benchmark in assessments, for example human oversight on the RAG pilot. In short, it's a risk-based law with four tiers..."
quiz.explanation: Honest about the legal scope, then pivots straight into demonstrating knowledge.

quiz.question: "Did you build the governance dashboard?"
quiz.answer: "I built the controls-testing MI in Excel. On the AI pilots I defined the KRIs and thresholds; engineering implemented the monitoring."
quiz.explanation: Precisely scopes what you did vs what engineering did — don't overclaim.

quiz.question: "What have you done since April?"
quiz.answer: "Enterprise work with an AI governance platform for BFSI clients, plus independent AI governance consulting."
quiz.explanation: A gap in the CV timeline needs a ready, confident answer.

quiz.question: "Do you have other offers? Are you offer shopping?"
quiz.answer: "I'm in a few conversations. This role is my priority because it's pure AI governance advisory." No details, no stories.
quiz.explanation: Brief and confident — don't over-explain or justify.

quiz.question: "Why AIGP before mastering the basics?"
quiz.answer: Avoid by passing Layer 1 first. If asked anyway: "AIGP is how I'm structuring the fundamentals," then prove it with a crisp answer.
quiz.explanation: The best defence against this question is simply being fluent in Layer 1.

quiz.question: "Why consulting rather than in-house?"
quiz.answer: "I've seen the in-house first-line view at Barclays and the vendor view selling a platform. Advisory is where both meet, and breadth across clients builds expertise faster."
quiz.explanation: Frames your varied background as a deliberate asset, not a gap.

quiz.question: "Your AI governance experience is under 4 years"
quiz.answer: "AI governance is risk and controls discipline applied to a new technology. I have that discipline from a G-SIB, plus live AI pilot assessments."
quiz.explanation: Reframes the objection around transferable discipline rather than defending the raw years.

stops.artifactPrompt: Record yourself delivering the 60-second intro from memory, without notes, timed. Then record yourself answering 3 of the 7 tricky questions above, also from memory. Listen back for 'to be honest', rushed pacing, and self-rejection.
